parts.title: My lucky number
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
For as long as I can remember, my lucky number has been seven. I was born on the seventh of July, my house is number seven, and I once won a prize in a raffle with ticket number seventy-seven. My friends say that this is just a coincidence, but I am not so sure.

Before every football match, I follow the same routine. I put my left boot on first, I tie the laces twice, and I touch the goalpost before I step onto the pitch. If I forget one of these things, I feel that something bad will happen. Last season I forgot to tie my laces twice and we lost five-nil, though the other team was very good.

My coach does not agree with me. He says that good players make their own luck by training hard. He is probably right, and I do train three times a week. But I still do my routine, because it makes me feel calm.

The funny thing is that I am not the only one. Half of the players in my team have a lucky charm, and one boy never washes his shirt during the season. I try to sit far from him on the bus.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer like the number seven?
options: It appears often in his life
It is the number on his shirt
His coach chose it for him
questions.explanation: He was born on the seventh, lives at number seven and won a prize with ticket seventy-seven.

questions.prompt: What does the writer do before a match?
options: He talks to the other team
questions.explanation: He follows the same routine before every match.

questions.prompt: What happened when he forgot to tie his laces twice?
options: He was dropped from the team
questions.explanation: They lost five-nil.

questions.prompt: What does his coach believe?
options: Routines are a waste of time
questions.explanation: He says that good players make their own luck by training hard.

questions.prompt: Why does he sit far from one boy on the bus?
options: The boy always talks about luck
The boy never washes his shirt
questions.explanation: The boy never washes his shirt during the season.

parts.title: Strange beliefs around the world
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Superstitions are found in every country, and many of them are very old. [1] In Britain, for example, people say that walking under a ladder brings bad luck.

Some beliefs are about animals. In many countries, a black cat that crosses your path is a bad sign. [2] But in the United Kingdom, a black cat is thought to bring good luck.

Some are about numbers. In Italy, seventeen is thought to be unlucky. [3] Many hotels in Italy have no room with that number.

Other beliefs are about food. In Japan, you should never stick your chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice. [4] It looks like something that is done at a funeral.

Many people laugh at these beliefs. [5] Still, they often do them just in case, because nobody wants to take a risk.
sentences: The reason is that the Roman numerals can be rearranged to mean "I have lived".
Few people can say exactly where such ideas started.
Our grandparents often told us stories of this kind.
It is rude, and that is why people avoid it.
They admit that there is no proof that they work.
Sailors, however, consider it a sign of good fortune.

gaps.explanation: Few people can say where ideas started, which fits "many of them are very old"; the ladder example follows.
Sailors consider the cat a good sign, which leads to the contrast in the United Kingdom.
The reason is about Roman numerals, and the next sentence says hotels have no such room.
It is rude, and the next sentence says it looks like something at a funeral.
They admit there is no proof, and "Still" in the next sentence shows the contrast.

parts.title: The four-leaf clover
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Many people believe that a four-leaf clover brings good luck. A normal clover has three leaves, so a four-leaf clover is quite rare. In fact, there is only [1] four-leaf clover for every ten thousand ordinary ones. People used to think that [2] you found one, you could see fairies. Today, people still collect them and put them inside books. Some even sell them [3] money. When I was small, my grandmother used to take me to the field behind her house. We looked for hours [4] we found a four-leaf clover. I have kept it in a frame ever since. I do not know whether it has really brought me luck, [5] it always reminds me of her. It is a lovely memory, and I think that this is the real reason why people like [6] kind of charm.

gaps.explanation: There is only one four-leaf clover for every ten thousand: the number.
If you found one, you could see fairies: a condition.
Sell them for money: the preposition for price.
Looked for hours until we found one: a limit in time.
Does not know whether it brought luck, but it reminds me of her: contrast.
This kind of charm: a determiner before kind.

parts.title: A talk about strange beliefs
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: nathalie
turns.text: Good afternoon. My name is Bree, and I study the history of beliefs. Today I would like to tell you about a few famous beliefs. First, the number thirteen. In many countries, buildings have no thirteenth floor. Some airplanes have no row thirteen, either. This fear is so common that it has a name. Second, the saying that a broken mirror brings seven years of bad luck. This idea comes from the Romans, who thought that the mirror held a part of your soul. Third, the custom of throwing salt over the left shoulder. People did this to send away the devil, because salt was precious. And finally, the belief that you should not open an umbrella indoors. It started in the eighteenth century, when umbrellas were large and could hurt people in small rooms. As you can see, many beliefs began as common sense. Thank you for listening.

gaps.explanation: I study the history of beliefs.

gaps.prompt: The saying about a broken mirror comes from the ___
gaps.explanation: This idea comes from the Romans.

gaps.prompt: People threw ___ over the left shoulder
gaps.explanation: The custom of throwing salt over the left shoulder.

gaps.prompt: The umbrella belief began in the ___ century
gaps.explanation: It started in the eighteenth century.
Many beliefs began as common sense.

parts.title: An interview with a goalkeeper
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Bram, many sports players have lucky habits. What are yours?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I always put on my left glove first, and I never step on the white line when I walk onto the pitch.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Where did these habits come from?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: From my first big match. I did these things by accident, and we won. Since then, I have never changed.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Have you ever forgotten to do them?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Once, in a cup match. I was so worried that I played badly, though in the end the team still won on penalties.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Does your team have any shared habits?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Yes, we all touch the same old ball before we leave the dressing room. It was the ball from our first win as a team.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Do you think that luck is more important than skill?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: No. Skill and training matter much more. But a good-luck habit helps me to feel calm, and that is useful too.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What advice would you give to young players?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Enjoy the game, work hard, and do not worry about small things. A good friend in the team is worth more than any charm.
